title: ControlNet as Topology — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of ControlNet as Topology's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier: a terrain you can carve that walks up from one ball to the test of denoise against weight, the noise schedule taken apart by scale beside a control image, and the GenAI Camera's depth sweeps laid beside the pose-versus-depth rule they test, with the fingerprint of the words each was laid against. I grow when the page is rewritten or a piece has something new to test; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.section: The same truth, made precise: the landscape
offers.what: "it shrinks the fog hiding the fine terrain until only the deepest basin remains" and "letting a ball roll into the deepest valley" describe an optimiser, not this cooling. The carving ends with the fog gone, not the temperature at zero, so it samples the terrain: each valley ends with about its share of the images, whatever its depth. Measured in the landscape piece, step 2 (checks.mjs, 2000 balls): the deepest valley (portrait, E −2.44) caught 17.3% for an 18% share; the shallowest, widest (mountains, E −0.53) caught 28.1% for a 30% share, the most of any. Proposed: "…until each ball is held by one basin: which one is chance, weighted by how much of the terrain the basin holds, not how deep it goes", and "letting a ball roll into a valley". CFG at high w is what pulls toward fewer, deeper valleys (lion valleys 24.8% at w 0, 99.2% at w 3).

offers.section: The same truth, made precise: the landscape
offers.what: "Denoise strength × ControlNet weight": the high-denoise half holds in the page's own picture and the low-denoise half does not, as written. From an init in one valley, 100 balls a square (landscape piece, step 5; checks.mjs): at denoise 1.0 the canyon caught 0% at weight 0.5, 78% at 3, 100% at 8, so only a deep enough canyon wins. But at low denoise the canyon does not compete evenly with the valley; it isn't felt at all unless it lies within about the fog's width at the start. A canyon 0.63 from the init caught 0% at every weight up to 12 for denoise 0.5 and below (start fog σ 0.08); one 0.26 away caught 0% at 0.3 and below, at most 6% at 0.4. And with the canyon beside the init, more denoise is not more armature: at weight 2 it caught 75% at denoise 0.7 against 45% at 1.0, since full denoise forgets an init that lay near the canyon. Proposed: "Denoise sets how far the armature can reach; weight sets how hard it holds once it does. High denoise lifts the ball into fog wide enough to feel the canyon from anywhere, and a deep enough canyon then wins every ball. Low denoise keeps the ball's reach to its own valley: a canyon cut through that valley competes with its texture, one cut elsewhere is never felt." Not tested on a network: this is the page's picture run exactly, and the GenAI Camera's runs (denoise 0.9, init and control from one Blender render) are the case of a canyon cut through the init's valley.

"it's the noise schedule cooling, coarse structure first and fine texture last" holds, but the schedule is not what orders it. The noise is white, the same power at every scale; the order comes from the picture, whose power falls with fineness. Measured in the rough-to-fine piece (checks.mjs), on Stable Diffusion's σ 14.6 to 0.03 with Karras's curve: the page's hero (spectral slope −2.66) has waves 4 across the frame decided at 10% of the strokes, 9 at 25%, 25 at 50%, 85 at 75%, every scale at 82%; a GenAI Camera render (slope −2.43) runs the same way. A control image with the same spread and a flat spectrum has nothing decided until 54% and every scale by 55%. Proposed: "…it's the noise schedule cooling against a picture whose coarse shapes are far louder than its fine ones: coarse structure first, fine texture last." The crossing is what the noise alone permits; a real denoiser can guess some detail earlier from the shape it already has.

offers.section: Pose vs depth — canyons of different shape (2026-07-09)
offers.what: The rule stands, but the example the section tells ran on a pose plate the GenAI Camera's own record later found too thin to bite: render 011 (13:01, pose-only figures) carries the caveat "clothing + stance came mostly from the img2img init at high denoise, not the pose", and render 020 is the diagnosis (the thin plate let the arms drift; the controlnet_aux plate held them). So in 011 what freed the costume was dropping depth, not adding pose. The re-run with the real plate is renders 021 (sorceress) and 022 (barbarian): pose held at 0.9, denoise 0.9, depth swept 0 to 0.8. Robes and fur at pose only and at depth 0.15; thinning by 0.30; at 0.60 and 0.80 both figures are bare, the costume pinned to the mannequin's surface. Proposed: cite renders 021 and 022 for the rule, and add that depth's weight is the dial: "how tight a canyon you want" is, for depth, how much weight you give it.

pieces.near: And you work the way every carver works
pieces.title: rough to fine · four steps
pieces.caption: **The first strokes commit the pose: tested, and given its reason.** Built up from the raw block of noise: one stroke of fog with the best guess under it, the scales the picture is made of against the noise floor, and last the whole schedule beside a control image with no coarse shape. Coarse is decided before fine at every stroke for the page's hero and for a GenAI Camera render; the control gets nothing until halfway, then everything at once. The fog is the same at every scale, so the order is the picture's, not the schedule's.

sections.heading: The same truth, made precise: the landscape

pieces.file: ControlNet as Topology — rich — the landscape.html
pieces.title: the landscape · five steps
pieces.caption: **An energy landscape you can carve.** One ball rolls down one valley; fog over six valleys cools rough to fine; CFG leans on the commission *a lion* and never lands a ball where no valley was; ControlNet carves a canyon there and takes them; last, the test of denoise against weight from one init, a map of a hundred balls a square. High denoise lets a deep enough canyon win, as the page says. Low denoise does not make the canyon compete evenly: it shortens its reach, and a canyon out of reach is never felt. It also checks the fog: balls end in every valley by its size, not only in the deepest.

sections.heading: Pose vs depth — canyons of different shape (2026-07-09)

pieces.title: depth strength sweep · sorceress · GenAI Camera render 021
pieces.near: A nude mannequin conditioned on depth
pieces.caption: **The rule, tested by sweep.** Top row is what was sent in: the mannequin, its pose skeleton (the real controlnet_aux plate), its depth. Below, pose held at 0.9 and denoise at 0.9 while depth's weight rises: pose only and 0.15 grow a full hooded robe; by 0.30 the legs are bare; at 0.60 and 0.80 the figure is the mannequin's surface, inked. Depth's weight is how tight the canyon is.

pieces.caption: The same sweep for the barbarian: fur mantle, cloak and boots at pose only; the fur thins as depth rises; at 0.60 and 0.80 only a loincloth survives on the mannequin's body. Two prompts, one shape of answer.

pieces.caption: The pose side, with the record's own caveat: this ran on the thin pose plate, and the robes and fur came mostly from the image-to-image init with depth gone, not from the pose.
